title: Institutional Construction: How to Catch HVAC and Electrical Scope Gaps in Complex Spec Sets
summary: Institutional spec sets bury HVAC and electrical scope gaps that become change orders. Here is how GCs catch them before bid day.
body_markdown:
## TL;DR


- Institutional projects carry some of the most complex MEP spec sets in ICI construction. HVAC and electrical scope gaps are routine, and they are expensive.
- The root causes are consistent: specs split across multiple divisions, addenda that modify only one section, and boilerplate scope sheets that miss project-specific callouts.
- Catching gaps before bid day requires reading drawings and specs together, not separately.
- Provision's[Scope Agent](https://provision.com/scope-agent) and[RFI Agent](https://provision.com/rfi-agent) review the full document set at once, source-tracing every finding to the exact page and section.


Canadian institutional construction is accelerating. The Dodge Momentum Index recorded a 4.9% rise in institutional planning in August 2026. Projects like the NAIT Advanced Skills Centre signal what is coming down the pipeline: large, complex, technically demanding builds where the spec sets run to thousands of pages and the MEP scope is anything but simple.


For GCs bidding institutional work, that complexity is a risk multiplier. HVAC and electrical scope gaps that might cost $20,000 on a commercial fit-out can reach six or seven figures on a hospital or post-secondary campus build. And they are almost never random. They are caused by the same habits, in the same places, on nearly every project.


This article breaks down where those gaps hide and what a disciplined pre-construction team does to catch them before they become change orders.


---


## Why Institutional Spec Sets Create More Scope Risk


Institutional projects are not just bigger versions of commercial work. They carry a different kind of specification complexity that magnifies scope risk at every stage.


### Multi-Division MEP Specs With No Single Owner


On a standard commercial project, HVAC scope is mostly in Division 23. Electrical is mostly in Division 26. But on an institutional project, that scope bleeds across divisions. Fire alarm interfaces live in Division 28. Building automation and controls span 23 and 25. Lighting controls touch 26 and 25. No single trade owns the full picture.


When an estimator reviews those divisions in isolation, the gaps appear in the white space between them. The spec says the mechanical contractor provides the BAS points. It does not say who wires them. That question costs money if it is not answered before bid day.


### Addenda Arrive Late and Modify Specific Sections


Institutional projects routinely issue multiple addenda. Each one may modify a single clause in one spec section. If your team is managing addenda manually, the chance that a modification to Section 23 81 19 gets cross-referenced against the electrical drawings and the control sequences is low. The chance it gets missed is high.


As one Estimating Manager at a Canadian ICI GC put it: *"If you miss anything, they'll bill it."* On institutional work, that is not a hypothetical. It is a weekly occurrence on poorly scoped projects.


### Owner-Specified Equipment With Unclear Responsibility Splits


Hospitals and post-secondary institutions often specify owner-furnished, contractor-installed equipment. The spec names the equipment. It does not always name who provides the conduit, the disconnect, the final connection, or the commissioning. Each of those items is a potential gap. Each one can be claimed by the mechanical or electrical sub as excluded if it is not in the scope package.


---


## The Most Common HVAC Scope Gaps in Institutional Specs


Provision's pre-construction research and the operator interviews behind the[Scope Gap Playbook's trade-specific chapter](https://provision.com/ebooks/scope-gap-playbook/trade-specific-scope-gaps) point to the same recurring gaps on institutional mechanical scope.


### Generator Field Conditioning


Emergency generators on institutional projects require field conditioning before they can be commissioned. This work includes load bank testing, temperature controls, and sometimes extended run cycles. It is frequently missing from both the mechanical and electrical scope sheets. Each sub assumes the other is carrying it. Neither is.


The Scope Gap Playbook flags generator field conditioning as one of the most recurring MEP anti-patterns in ICI construction. When it surfaces post-award, it surfaces as a change order.


### Motor Starters and VFD Scope Splits


The mechanical spec calls for a fan or pump with a variable frequency drive. The electrical spec covers the panel. Who supplies the VFD? Who installs it? Who provides the interconnecting wiring between the drive and the BAS? These questions seem simple. On institutional projects with dozens of VFDs, an unresolved split can represent significant cost.


### Fire-Rated Louvres and HVAC Penetrations


Institutional buildings have strict fire separations. HVAC penetrations through rated assemblies require fire dampers, interlocks, and in some cases, rated duct wrap. The spec may call this out in Division 07 (Thermal and Moisture Protection) rather than Division 23. If the mechanical estimator is not reading Division 07, the fire damper scope lands in a gap.


### BAS Points and Control Wiring


Building automation scope is one of the most reliably misscoped items on institutional projects. The mechanical spec covers the control devices. The electrical spec covers power. The BAS spec (Division 25) covers the network. But the low-voltage control wiring between those three systems is often described in none of them clearly enough to avoid a dispute at buyout.


---


## The Most Common Electrical Scope Gaps in Institutional Specs


### Lighting Controls and Occupancy Sensor Wiring


Institutional projects commonly specify daylight harvesting, occupancy-based dimming, and scheduled switching. The electrical drawings show fixtures. The spec shows controls. But the wiring between the lighting control panels, the occupancy sensors, and the dimming drivers is frequently not drawn. It is described in a spec section that the electrical estimator may not cross-reference against the fixture schedule.


### IT and AV Rough-In Scope


Post-secondary and healthcare projects carry significant IT and AV infrastructure. The electrical sub is typically responsible for conduit, back boxes, and rough-in. The AV contractor handles the systems. When the scope sheets do not define the exact rough-in responsibility, both subs price it, or neither does. The gap becomes visible during buyout.


### Emergency Power System Scope Splits


Institutional projects require life-safety branch, critical branch, and equipment branch circuits. The transfer switch scope, the ATS wiring, and the tie-ins to the generator are described in multiple spec sections. When the electrical scope sheet just says "emergency power system," the sub will price the minimum. The gap will be visible in the first progress claim.


### Commissioning and Witness Testing


Many institutional owners now require witnessed commissioning for electrical systems: switchgear testing, UPS verification, and emergency system load tests. These requirements often appear in a commissioning spec (Division 01 40 00) rather than in Division 26. If the electrical scope sheet does not explicitly include commissioning obligations, the sub will exclude them.


---


## Where the Scope Review Process Breaks Down


The gap between what the spec requires and what the scope package captures is almost never an accident. It follows from a small set of habits that experienced pre-construction teams have already identified.


### Reviewing Divisions in Isolation


The most common anti-pattern in institutional MEP review is reading each spec division in a silo. An estimator reviews Division 23 and writes the mechanical scope. A different estimator reviews Division 26 and writes the electrical scope. Nobody reads them against each other, against the drawings, or against Division 25. The white space stays white.


The Scope Gap Playbook's Eight Habits frame this clearly: Habit 1 is drawings-first, not boilerplate-first. The same principle applies to spec review. Start with what the drawings actually show. Then reconcile the spec against the drawings. Then reconcile the divisions against each other.


### Using Boilerplate Scope Sheets


Boilerplate scope sheets are a floor, not a ceiling. That is Habit 4. On a standard commercial project, a boilerplate HVAC scope may cover 80% of what the spec requires. On an institutional project with a chilled water plant, a BAS integration requirement, and owner-furnished AHUs, that same boilerplate covers far less. The gaps are project-specific. The scope sheet needs to be too.


### Missing the Addenda Cascade


Addenda on institutional projects do not arrive as a package. They arrive one at a time, targeting specific sections. When the team is managing addenda manually, the cascade is easy to lose. A revised control sequence in Addendum 3 may change what the electrical sub is responsible for in a way that is not reflected in the scope package issued to that sub.


This is not a process failure. It is a document volume problem. Institutional projects may issue five, six, or eight addenda before close. Manual reconciliation across thousands of spec pages is where gaps get embedded.


---


## How to Catch HVAC and Electrical Scope Gaps Before Bid Day


The following steps reflect what high-performing pre-construction teams at ICI GCs do consistently. They match the Eight Habits framework from the Scope Gap Playbook.


### Step 1: Read Drawings and Specs Together, Not Sequentially


Start with the mechanical and electrical drawings. Identify every system. Then find the spec section that governs each system. Cross-reference them explicitly. If the drawing shows a chilled water plant and the spec describes it in both Division 23 and Division 25, both sections need to be in the scope review before you write a single line of scope.


### Step 2: Map the Division Boundaries for MEP


Create a simple map of which divisions govern which systems on this specific project. Mark every boundary where two divisions share responsibility. Those boundaries are where scope gaps live. They deserve a dedicated review step, not an assumption that the sub will figure it out.


### Step 3: Track Addenda Against the Scope Package


When an addendum arrives, the first question is: does this change any item already in the scope package? If the answer is yes, the scope package needs to be updated before it goes to subs. This sounds obvious. It is frequently skipped under bid-day time pressure.


### Step 4: Issue Trade-Specific Scope Packages That Name the Gaps


A scope package that says "as per plans and specs" is the most-cited anti-pattern in GC pre-construction. The Scope Gap Playbook quotes one Pre-Construction Lead at a Top-ENR Canadian GC on this directly: getting to the right level of detail means being as specific as a recipe. If the scope does not name the responsibility, the sub will not carry it.


Trade-specific scope packages for institutional HVAC and electrical work should name: the BAS scope split, the VFD responsibility, the commissioning obligation, and the fire damper scope. Every item that could reasonably be claimed as excluded needs to be explicitly included or explicitly excluded.


### Step 5: Run a Pre-Issue Review Checkpoint


Habit 8 in the Scope Gap Playbook is the pre-issue scope review checkpoint. Before the scope package goes to subs, one more person reads it against the drawings and the most recent addendum. This is not a full re-review. It is a targeted check for items that changed in the last addendum cycle. On institutional projects, this step catches a material number of gaps.

## Frequently Asked Questions


### What makes institutional construction HVAC and electrical scope review harder than commercial work?


Institutional projects split MEP scope across Divisions 23, 25, 26, and 28. No single trade owns the full picture. Addenda arrive frequently and modify individual sections. When teams review divisions in isolation, the gaps form in the white space between them, and those gaps become change orders after award.


### What are the most common HVAC scope gaps on institutional projects?


Generator field conditioning, motor starter and VFD responsibility splits, BAS control wiring, and fire damper scope in fire-rated penetrations are the most recurring gaps. They appear consistently because they sit at the boundary between two or more spec divisions and are not clearly owned by any single trade in the scope package.


### What are the most common electrical scope gaps on institutional projects?


Lighting control wiring, IT and AV rough-in responsibility, emergency power system scope splits, and commissioning and witness testing requirements. Commissioning obligations often appear in Division 01 rather than Division 26, so electrical estimators miss them if they are not reading the full spec set.


### How do addenda create scope gaps on institutional projects?


Institutional projects routinely issue multiple addenda, each targeting a specific spec section. When teams manage addenda manually, a modification to one section may not be reconciled against related sections or the scope package already issued to subs. The gap embeds at the addendum boundary and surfaces after award.


### What is the "as per plans and specs" anti-pattern?


"As per plans and specs" is the most-cited scope writing anti-pattern among GC pre-construction teams. It transfers all interpretation risk to the sub, who will then price the minimum they can defensibly claim is included. On institutional projects, this language routinely produces disputed change orders on MEP items that were never explicitly scoped.
